topic: the physics of a bed of nails — why 1,000 nails don't hurt but one does
title: 1,000 Nails Won't Cut You — One Will (Same Body Weight)
description: Why a bed of a thousand nails won't hurt you but stepping on just one will — the physics of pressure, explained in under 20 seconds. AI-narrated science commentary.

hook_candidates.text: A bed of 1,000 nails won't break your skin — step on just one, same body weight, and you're bleeding.
Why can someone lie down on hundreds of sharp nails and stand back up without a single cut?
The bed-of-nails trick isn't about tough skin — it's a math problem, not a stunt.

payoff_mechanism: Pain and puncturing both depend on pressure, which is force divided by the area it's spread over — one nail concentrates your full body weight onto a single sharp point, but a thousand nails divide that same weight across a thousand points, so the force landing on each tip drops below what's needed to break skin.

beats.text: A bed of **1,000** nails won't cut you — one nail will.
Because pressure is about **area**: one nail puts your whole weight on one point, a thousand nails spread it so thin nothing breaks skin.
Not the **1,000** you'd worry about — it's the one. Follow for more.
